title: The Oldest Signs of Belief
objective: After this level you can describe what ancient burials with grave goods and the stone pillars of Göbekli Tepe suggest about religion before writing.
summary: About 100,000 years ago at Qafzeh, people buried their dead with ochre and antlers. Göbekli Tepe's carved pillars, raised by hunter-gatherers, show ritual on a grand scale long before writing.

cards.headline: Writing began around 3200 BCE. Signs of belief are far older.
cards.body: For the long ages before writing, archaeologists read what people left behind. The oldest clues are graves, some about 100,000 years old. The grandest is a hilltop of carved stone pillars.

cards.headline: A child buried with antlers
cards.body: At Qafzeh cave in Israel, about 100,000 years ago, early modern humans buried their dead. Red ochre lay near the bones, which suggests it was used in a ritual. In one grave, a youngster of about 12 or 13 lay in a pit with two deer antlers placed on the chest. Researchers call it a deliberate, ceremonial burial. Someone chose those antlers.

cards.headline: What a grave can and can't tell you
cards.body: Early humans often buried their dead with beads and other symbolic objects. The Smithsonian's scientists suggest these rituals may imply a belief that a person's identity continues beyond death. Notice the "may". A grave keeps the gifts, not the thoughts behind them, so archaeologists speak carefully.

cards.headline: Stone circles before farms
cards.body: In southeastern Turkey, in the 10th to 9th millennium BCE, people who had not yet taken up farming raised Göbekli Tepe. Its T-shaped limestone pillars reach over 5 meters tall and weigh up to 50 tons, and some are carved with foxes, scorpions and lions. Hunter-gatherers built this. Whatever they believed, they believed it enough to move mountains, or at least 50-ton pieces of them.

cards.headline: Temple, town, or both?
cards.body: Its excavator, Klaus Schmidt, saw Göbekli Tepe as a ritual center where no one lived. Newer digs found hearths, houses and a rainwater cistern, so scholars now see a settlement with a religious center. Before writing, the evidence can be read in more than one way, and each season of digging can change the reading.

cards.headline: The Oldest Signs of Belief: the takeaways
learned: About 100,000 years ago at Qafzeh, people buried their dead with ochre and antlers
Grave goods may point to belief in life beyond death
Hunter-gatherers raised Göbekli Tepe's pillars before farming

questions.prompt: Who raised the carved stone pillars of Göbekli Tepe?

options.label: Hunter-gatherers who had not yet taken up farming
Roman engineers from Asia Minor
options.rationale: It's many thousands of years older than Rome.

options.label: Early farmers living in walled cities
options.rationale: Its builders hadn't yet taken up farming.

options.label: Sumerian scribes who kept temple records
options.rationale: It predates writing by thousands of years.

questions.explanation: Göbekli Tepe was built in the 10th to 9th millennium BCE by hunter-gatherers before farming.

questions.prompt: What might beads and symbolic objects in ancient graves imply, according to the Smithsonian?

options.label: That the dead were powerful rulers or chiefs
A belief that identity continues beyond death
That writing already existed
options.rationale: These burials came long before writing.

options.label: That the dead had been traders

questions.explanation: Such rituals may imply a belief that a person's identity extends beyond death; the 'may' matters.

questions.prompt: What do the Qafzeh graves and Göbekli Tepe have in common as evidence?

options.label: Both are written records of early prayers
Both were built by the first farmers
options.rationale: Göbekli Tepe's builders weren't farmers yet.

options.label: Both point to ritual long before writing

questions.explanation: Ochre and antlers at Qafzeh and the carved pillars at Göbekli Tepe both suggest ritual thousands of years before writing began around 3200 BCE.
